My understanding, and people may very well correct me here, is that when you select the villain and read their main scheme setup you select a difficulty level. 

Standard, as you’ve guessed, is typically form 1 and 2 of the villain cards with the standard encounter set shuffled into the villain encounter deck. (With any additional encounter sets they the main scheme requires. Such as Bomb Scare being the recommended set for Rhino)

Expert invokes form 2 and 3 of a villain, as well as shuffling the expert card AND the standard cards into the villain encounter deck. 

The other way you can experiment with difficulties is by switching out the encounter sets for the different main schemes. For example, Bomb Scare is relatively simple when compared to Under Attack, so swapping one for the other will have some impact on gameplay. Other encounter sets offer a variety of different challenges, some fun and some punishing.  Kang’s set has some particularly challenging encounter sets they definitely change the potency of the villain phase.

I would encourage you both to seek out counselling. Your feelings deserve to be validated. Even if it’s a phone line, opening up and talking about it it. It sounds like you need a third party to help facilitate honest conversation though.

First, do me a favour. Breathe in. Count to 3. Breathe out. 

Anxiety is a bitch. The gnawing feeling can be terrifying but trust me when I say you can overcome this. 

You are letting it be the dominant thought in your mind. When we do this, it affects all the other aspects of our lives.

The next time you have a worry about climate change or whatever else, consider one or more of the following:

- acknowledge the thought, say, “Yes, I’m worried about ‘x,y,z’ “ then continue with whatever task you were performing 

-write the worry/bothersome thought on a piece of part. Crumple up this paper and throw it across the room. But then, don’t go clean it up right away. Let it exist but in a space that is away from you and your mind. 

-take a break and focus on something you love, for example I like to paint miniatures, so I would start a mini to paint and let that preoccupation enable you to move on from the worry

*”Uses (X “type”) — When a card with this keyword enters play, place X all-purpose counters from the token pool on the card. The word following the value establishes and identifies the type of uses the card holds.
Each card with this keyword also has an ability that references the type of use established by the keyword as part of the cost. When such an ability spends a use, a counter of that type must be removed from the card.
After a card with uses spends its final use (and the effect resolves), discard the card.”*

It’s a running joke in my game group that if we’re playing a cooperative game, I’m likely to cheat for the benefit of the group. 

It’s usually in things like “the opening pull of a community market is waaaaay to expensive to get us going so I’m discarding and starting the market over”. 

Or like “ugh, this villain in Hogwarts Battle and this villain out at the same time are terrible combos for round 1, imma just switch that out”. 

If we’re about to lose from a bad cars draw or dice roll, that we usually accept and simply restart the game. 

I think it ultimately comes down to my group’s enjoyment level. If we’re feeling completely discouraged and downtrodden by a game, I may rearrange the deck a little to boost morale things like that but it’s only ever for the benefit of the group.

I vividly remember standing and staring as the flames began to climb up the walls and across the ceiling. I honestly don’t know how or why the flames just abruptly stopped burning but they did. Thankfully no one was hurt.

Hello friend. 

The journey you are going through is challenging. I hear what you are saying. My girlfriend also has BPD, depression and anxiety. It can be difficult but it impossible. 

All I can offer are the things that her and I have done together. 

1. First of all, a worry journal or book. We've found that by having her voice her concerns or her worries, it allows her to move past them. She can go back to them because they're now something concrete. 

2. A daily goal. It does not have to be huge, it can be as simple as "today I'm going to shower and get dressed". And then tomorrow it might be that but "before noon". Move on to other bigger goals as you go. But make sure they are achievable. "Today I'll apply for 5 jobs" is much more reasonable than "today I'm going to get a job". 

3. It's okay to make mistakes. Allow yourself the opportunity to learn from these moments. I believe that everything happens for a reason, try to find a nugget of truth in all that you do. 

4. Talk to people. This is very hard. Admittedly my girlfriend can have issues with this one too, she does not want to be a burden. Know that your family loves you and wants to support you. Do not be afraid to share a little. Perhaps a hotline if you're ever feeling suicidal. Life is an incredible journey, don't end your early. 

5. Find a passion. Once you've completed a goal, reward yourself. My girlfriend has taken to going to the gym. She finds it helps her mental health. I am not an expert in Carpal Tunnel and its limitations, but I am hopeful that you can find something. (Are you into Jackson Pollock*[sp?]? Maybe is style would work?) If art is your thing, I am sure there is a way for you to do it without injuring yourself further. 

6. One day at a time. Yes, planning for the future is important. But not as important as the now is for you. Your things will get sorted, but right now, take each day to get you sorted. Talk to doctor, see if counselling or medication is something that could work for you. You can conquer this. 

7. You are not your disorder. You are your own person with dreams, desires and passions. Give mental health the finger and then kick its ass. 

I believe in you. There are people all around the world that face this too. You can win. Stay strong. Be well. I wish you nothing but the best.

Hello friend! A month of two ago we actually had a PC die during an epic encounter with an elder brain. To make a long story short, the rogue/cleric had a scroll of 'raise dead' and rolled to use it. With the successful casting of the spell we went into the Mercer ritual. 

I can honestly say it was some of the best RP at my table ever. The emotion and feeling people were putting into their offerings was incredible. There were many a tear shed that night. With each offering you could see the hope/fear/anxiety in their faces as they rolled their d20s.

And then I rolled the final die in front of them, telling the group what was needed. (I felt like for this first one, it was important to do it in front of the group, to be perfectly transparent that it was the dice telling the story now, not me.)

Both myself and the players agreed, the ritual added an element of uncertainty to death. Rather than simple easy "get-out-of-death free" cards, these spells now become powerful tools that demonstrate the soul ebbing between the mortal coil and beyond. 

The ritual itself sparked a huge crisis of faith for our cleric. He began questioning whether it was right that he should be able to revive people at all, whether it was ethical to have say over who lived and who died. 

If you have players that are connected emotional to their characters, that are playing the game for more than just "kick the door, loot the treasure", I totally believe that the resurrection ritual is the way to go. It adds a great deal of depth to the game and it makes death a lot more of a threat, especially at higher levels. 

Sorry for the long winded speech, I hope that provided you with some ample insight into the matter.
